question.explanation:
Let $g(x)=2x-11$ and $f(g(x)) = g(x)^{6}.$

Differentiating, we have \begin{align*} f'(g(x)) & = ( g^{6})' = 6g^{5}, \\ g'(x) & = (2x-11)' = 2. \end{align*}

Then, using the chain rule,

\begin{align*} f'(x) & = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\\ & = 6g^{5} \cdot 2\\ & = 12(2x-11)^5. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=4.$
question.explanation:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}. \]

Let $u=2x+1.$ Then $y =\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \]

and

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2. \]

Multiplying the two together gives

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \cdot 2\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt {2x+1}}.\\ \end{align*}

Finally, substituting $x = 4,$ we get \begin{align*} \left.\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}\right|_{x=4} &=\left.\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\right)\right|_{x=4}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2(4)+1}}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} . \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Let $g(x)=6x-5$ and $f(g(x)) = g(x)^{6}.$

Differentiating, we have \begin{align*} f'(g(x)) & = ( g^{6})' = 6g^{5}, \\[5pt] g'(x) & = (6x-5)' = 6. \end{align*}

Then, using the chain rule, \begin{align*} f'(x) & = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x) \\[5pt] & = 6g^{5} \cdot (6) \\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{36(6x-5)^5}. \end{align*}
